Best,
Dr. Rivera

Please schedule an appointment (video or in-person) within the next 2–4 weeks so we can go over your home glucose log, diet, and medications together and make a clear, step-by-step plan.

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi John,

In the first few weeks after starting sertraline, it’s fairly common to notice temporary side effects such as feeling more restless, changes in sleep, or feeling more keyed up. I don’t want you to stop the sertraline on your own right now, since we’re still in the early adjustment period, but I do think we should adjust our approach. I’d also recommend keeping a consistent sleep and wake schedule, avoiding screens and work emails for at least an hour before bed, limiting caffeine after noon, and avoiding large or late meals right before bedtime.

If you notice any severe side effects such as thoughts of harming yourself, feeling out of control, or intense agitation you can’t manage, please call our office right away or go to the nearest emergency room.

Please send me an update in about 1–2 weeks to let me know how your sleep and anxiety are doing with these changes. Based on that, we can decide together whether to adjust the dose, switch medications, or consider a short-term sleep aid while we work on the underlying anxiety.

Dr. Rivera

Sam

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi Sam,

Thank you for your message and for explaining how much your knees have been affecting your work and daily activities.

From what you describe, it sounds like your osteoarthritis pain has progressed and is no longer well controlled with acetaminophen alone. The X-rays from 6 months ago already showed moderate to severe wear-and-tear changes, and it is common for symptoms to gradually worsen over time.

You have not done anything wrong or “waited too long”—these changes tend to build up over years, and our goal now is to find the best combination of treatments to help you function as well as possible.

In addition to acetaminophen, options we can consider include topical anti-inflammatory gel applied to the knees, a supervised physical therapy program to strengthen the muscles around the joint, a knee brace for support, and, if appropriate given your other health conditions, short courses of an oral anti-inflammatory medication. In some cases, steroid injections into the knee can also provide temporary relief.

Knee replacement surgery is usually considered when pain is significantly limiting daily activities and more conservative measures are no longer helping, but it is not the only option and it is not something we would rush into without a full evaluation.

Please schedule an appointment with me in the next 2–4 weeks so we can examine your knees, review your prior imaging, and talk through these options in more detail. In the meantime, continue using acetaminophen as directed (not exceeding the total daily dose we discussed), try to avoid activities that involve prolonged kneeling or squatting, and use ice packs after heavier activity if that provides relief.

Best,
Dr. Rivera

It’s good to hear that you’re feeling better than you were at the time of the flare, but needing your rescue inhaler 2–3 times a day and still noticing chest tightness in the evenings suggests that your asthma is not yet fully under control.

Finishing the prednisone burst was appropriate after that more severe episode, and it can take some time for your airways to fully settle down. However, our goal is that you should not need your rescue inhaler that often on a regular basis.

For now, I’d like you to be very consistent with your fluticasone inhaler—2 puffs twice a day, every day, even when you feel well—and to use a spacer if you have one, as that can help the medicine reach your lungs more effectively. If you notice any severe symptoms such as marked difficulty breathing, trouble speaking in full sentences, using your neck or chest muscles to breathe, or your rescue inhaler not helping, please seek urgent or emergency care right away.

Otherwise, please keep a brief log over the next 1–2 weeks of how often you’re using your rescue inhaler, any nighttime symptoms (waking up coughing or short of breath), and any known triggers (like exercise or being around smoke), and send that to me in a follow-up message. Dr. Rivera

About two weeks ago I noticed a red, bumpy rash on the inside of my right forearm. At first it just looked a little dry and itchy, but over the last week it’s spread further down toward my wrist and up toward my elbow.

It’s pretty itchy, especially at night, and I’ve caught myself scratching it in my sleep. I tried some over-the-counter hydrocortisone cream and switching soaps, but it doesn’t seem to be going away.

I work in a warehouse and sometimes handle boxes that are dusty or have been in storage a long time, so I’m wondering if it could be something I’m coming into contact with. I’m also a bit worried it could be something more serious like shingles or some kind of skin cancer, even though it doesn’t really hurt, just itches.

I’m feeling a little self-conscious because it’s visible when I wear short sleeves, and a coworker asked me today if it was contagious, which freaked me out. Do I need to come in to have it looked at, or is there something stronger I can try at home?

Eric

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi Eric,

Thank you for your message and for explaining what has been going on with the rash on your arm.

Based on your description — an itchy, red, bumpy rash on the inner forearm that has been spreading slowly over about two weeks and is more itchy than painful — this sounds more consistent with a type of eczema or contact dermatitis than with shingles or skin cancer. Shingles usually causes clusters of painful blisters in a band on one side of the body, and skin cancers are typically not this itchy and generally don’t appear this suddenly.

Given that you work around dusty boxes and may be coming into contact with different materials, a contact reaction is possible. In addition to avoiding any obvious new products (such as soaps, lotions, or gloves) that might be irritating the skin, I’d suggest using a gentle fragrance-free moisturizer on the area twice daily and continuing a low-strength steroid cream for a short period.

If you’ve been using 1% hydrocortisone once or twice a day for a full 1–2 weeks without any improvement, or if the rash starts to blister, ooze, become very painful, or spread quickly, we should see you in person to examine it and consider a stronger prescription cream or other treatments.

Please also let us know right away if you develop fever, feel generally unwell, or notice red streaks going up the arm, as those would be reasons to be seen more urgently.

Otherwise, if the rash is not improving over the next 1–2 weeks despite gentle skin care and avoiding irritants, please schedule an in-person visit so we can take a closer look and make a plan.

Best,
Dr. Rivera

The only recent change I can think of is that we switched my blood pressure medicine to amlodipine a few weeks ago because of that cough. My home blood pressure readings have actually been better (around 128/78 most days), but now I’m afraid this new medicine is doing something bad to my heart.

Do I need to be seen urgently or go to the ER the next time this happens? I’m nervous to even go for a walk because I don’t want to trigger it.

[Dr. Rivera]: Hi Karen,

Thank you for your message and for describing these episodes in detail.

From what you’ve shared so far, these brief spells of heart pounding that resolve on their own after a few minutes, with your blood pressure otherwise well controlled and a normal EKG and labs at your last visit, are less suggestive of an immediate heart attack. However, it is important that we learn more about the pattern to decide what further evaluation is needed.

Amlodipine does not typically cause rapid heart rhythms, but some people can feel more aware of their heartbeat when starting a new blood pressure medication or when they are anxious about their heart. I’d like you to keep a simple log for the next 1–2 weeks: note the time of each episode, what you were doing right before it started, how long it lasts, and whether you have any associated symptoms such as chest pain, pressure, shortness of breath at rest, fainting, or pain going to your jaw or arm.

If at any point you develop severe chest pain or pressure, trouble breathing that does not improve quickly, fainting, or symptoms that feel very different or much more intense than what you’ve described, please call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room.

Otherwise, please send me the log after 1–2 weeks, and we can decide whether to bring you in sooner for an exam, repeat EKG, or consider a heart monitor to look for an abnormal rhythm. In the meantime, you can continue your amlodipine as prescribed, and it is generally safe to keep up with light to moderate walking as long as you stop and rest if you feel unwell.

Best,
Dr. Rivera
